Description: *Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata* (The Teaching of the Fierce Crow Goddess). This text is presented as a dialogue between Kākacaṇḍeśvarī—also known as Kākacāmuṇḍā—who is identified with Kaṅkālī (the Skeleton) and Kālarātrī (Dark Night), both manifestations of Kālī; and her consort, the five-headed Bhairava, who is likely Svacchandabhairava, a form of Bhairava associated in certain aspects with the deity of medicine. The two are seated upon Mount Kailāsa. Following the goddess’s request for the knowledge that leads to liberation, the deity promises to grant it and proceeds to teach the preparation of medicinal herbs for healing and magical purposes. He particularly emphasizes the magical preparation of alchemical mercury, thereby making this an important unpublished work on Indian alchemy (*rasāyana*).

Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
I ask Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods, who is preceded by Bhṛgu and others;
as well as Skanda and the rest, Mahāmāyā, and Bhṛṅgī, each individually.
Salutation to the illustrious Vakratuṇḍa.
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, accompanied by Umā,
the Preceptor of the World [spoke] regarding the Tantra of the Eight Yoginīs, which is the most secret of secrets.
O God, for the illumination of all knowledge, you who are the refuge of all-knowing ones—
how is it that this entire purpose has been placed by you entirely upon me?
The illustrious Lord said:
Kaṅkālī, Kālarātrī, Kākacaṇḍā, and Vacāṃvikā;
Kaṅkālī, Kālarātrī, and Kākacaṇḍeśvarī are thus considered.
Thus, the two [deities] were honored by the hosts of leaders of the Yoginīs with joyful songs, dances, instrumental music, and various words, as their hearts were filled with delight.
Then some, filled with joy, praised that Bhairava deity surrounded by the hosts of Yoginīs, while other Guhyakas also offered praise.
Some danced before him, and some performed laughter;
by these devotees of knowledge, Bhairava was worshipped there.
The Goddess said:
Having seen the terrifying god, five-faced and three-eyed,
who was joyful and honored by the three worlds, she spoke while bowing with her wife.
O Bhairava, when these [offerings] are worshipped there with knowledge and devotion,
the goddess Kākacaṇḍeśvarī, Umādevī, and Bhairavī [are pleased].

The illustrious Bhairava said: O Goddess, that which is eternal, the great knowledge free from fear, and the discourse on knowledge which was previously granted by Manu as the bestower of the accomplishment of immortality; [that I shall now explain].
This knowledge does not perceive those who follow the instructions of the conditions [of the Vedas];
because of the decay of the age of the Vedas, no accomplishment is found thereby.
Or else, O lady of beautiful hips, according to the Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata,
O Goddess, one should contemplate the entire liberated reality as being devoid of all limiting adjuncts.
Śrī Kākacaṇḍeśvarī said:
How does this life-principle (jīvaka), residing within the body, come to be designated as "life" (jīva)?
Why does it perform actions while situated within the cage of saṃsāra?
Seized by old age, disease, and poverty, and bound by the fetters of saṃsāra,
each person carries their own burden upon their shoulders alone.
O Śaṅkara, please tell me why many living beings in a single place utter the auspicious word "Jaya" (Victory) while performing one action or refraining from another.
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Kākacāmuṇḍā, my dear one, for the benefit of practitioners.
O fair-faced one, you have asked me for this speech which is more secret than the secret.
I shall speak in brief; listen, O Kākacaṇḍeśvarī! He who is the Self, the Supreme, eternal, and the Lord without beginning or end—him I shall describe.
Whether it be one's own nature or the state beyond qualities, free from all disease and affliction,
the body remains eternally situated within the connection to beginningless karma.
Action, consisting of the adjuncts of the individual soul, proceeds from ignorance;
therefore, one should diligently abandon action, for it is indeed served [practiced] within saṃsāra.
Deluded by desire, he performs various actions within saṃsāra;
for the sake of sensual enjoyment, he does not know the means of acquiring wealth.
She engages in agriculture, trade, and service; she performs the work of a master and a servant; and she carries burdens of wood and various loads of grass.
Through bodily austerity, he makes a means for obtaining sensual pleasures;
that man, though possessing wealth, performs various kinds of difficult labors.
And in this world of mortals, those who wander about thinking only of sensual pleasures and wealth are born with hearts afflicted by poverty.
They are born deaf, blind, lame, humpbacked, and crippled;
in this great cycle of existence, they are bound by the very quality [of their actions].
One who performs action immediately, yet is devoid of both ignorance and non-ignorance,
does not leave saṃsāra, even while remaining in the body or being free from the body.
O auspicious one, you have told this to those who inquire: that within the terrible cycle of existence, the flow of time is but a mere moment.
O blessed lady, why do you ask about one thing while I am speaking of another?
I shall certainly explain the scripture of Kākacaṇḍeśvarī to you.
Thus, according to the tradition of Kākacaṇḍeśvara.
Kākacaṇḍeśvarī said:
O Great God, O Supreme Lord, I shall explain that which accomplishes the enjoyment of desires, by means of which one attains wealth without affliction.
Therefore, I wish to hear this; please graciously explain the fivefold divine sandals, which are the means for accomplishing the desire for women.
Such is the collyrium and the pill for moving through the sky;
it is for the benefit of practitioners, enabling them to go among gods, upon the earth, and into the air.
He spoke of the "leech-bind" (jalukābandha), the elixir of the alchemists (dhātuvāda-rasāyana),
as well as the digestion (jāraṇa), the killing (māraṇa), and the liquefaction (drāvaṇa) of mica (abhraka).
2b) O Lord of Gods, O Destroyer of Tripura, tell me the means for this purpose;
O God, speak of the alchemical work (*rasakarma*) as it is the very essence.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Kākacāmuṇḍā, my dear one, for the benefit of practitioners;
I shall tell you in brief that which is the means for attaining the various siddhis.
Neither the attainment of material wealth, nor enjoyment, nor even desire is established for those devoid of substance;
lacking substance, they remain in the form of gods, humans, or ghosts.
Wandering through the world of mortals, they cause affliction to others;
they seize the life-force of both those who are alive and those who are dead.
Established in wisdom through the form of the enjoyment of time,
those devoid of substance do not shine, just as a body is without splendor when deprived of life.
Those afflicted with leprosy, those deprived of life, the mute, the blind, and likewise the deaf—
the God whose banner is the sea-monster (Kāmadeva) does not pursue them in this mortal world for the sake of wealth.
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall describe that [mantra] which accomplishes the Lord of the Gods, the King of Sages, for the benefit of practitioners, O Beloved.
Digestion (jāraṇa), killing (māraṇa), and so forth are the supreme means for preparing substances;
they arise as the means for enjoyment for the sake of attaining the perfection of mercury (rasa).
The Vajradaṇḍa, the Sudaṇḍa, and likewise the Lohadaṇḍa—
these three medicinal herbs are beneficial for the killing of mercury.
Vajradaṇḍa, Vajra, Lohadaṇḍa, and Vaṭa,
as well as Sudaṇḍa and Brahmadaṇḍa— these are briefly proclaimed as his beloved [sons].
The practitioner, with a joyful mind, should cause this to be grasped in brief;
having combined that which is endowed with essence, one should rub it together.
The blindfolded [substance] has been prepared and meditated upon; the mercury dies in an instant.
When the great elixir is perfected, I shall make it capable of piercing a thousand times.
One should smear a great medicinal herb previously taken with false speech;
this is the procedure for the binding of mercury, by which even a blind person becomes endowed with sight.
Afterwards, the wise one should add copper in thousands of palas;
having treated it with the group of acids, he should then treat it with the group of alkalis.
A person should rub [the substance] seven times with *vajrakṣīrā* and the milk of *arka*;
having performed a *puṭa* (roasting) in this manner, it will briefly become free of *kālikā*.
One should cause mercury to digest within the belly of a fool's womb in a fire of *svadira* wood;
one should then cast silver into it, and it becomes excellent.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata.
3b) Now I shall further explain this method for binding with clay: one should have the wise person take clay that is free from grass and stones. 1.
O Dear One, one should take two parts of [the substance] and earth as the third; having combined them, they should be kneaded and placed in a crucible.
O Dear One, it should be graspable by the breasts or circular; O Dear One, it is renowned as the "mouth-binding" [mudrā], which is beneficial for practitioners.
Then, O Goddess, O beloved, having taken the impurity of the horse and the elephant,
the practitioner should burn it, O lady of excellent hips, until it has been completely consumed by fire.
One who desires strength should grind the leaves of the vāsaka plant together with ant-hill earth using a pestle of water-reed.
Having added the impurities of horse and elephant, one should grind it with urine;
furthermore, one should prepare this crucible, the *cakratāla* [furnace], and the *mūṣaka* [crucible].
That [metal] also becomes like a diamond; this is proclaimed as *mūṣābandha*.
Having first performed these [preparations], one should thereafter commence the ritual work.
Thus have been described the crucible-piercings; now I shall further explain the procedure for the killing of mercury.
First, the adept of the deity should cause the herb to be ground three times;
he should smear the crucible with that and then begin the work of preparing the medicinal grain.
O beloved, one who performs the Kurukarma as desired dies quickly;
listen, O dear one, to how one becomes a maker of stars and a maker of gold in this world.
4a) Having fashioned a vessel made of iron and a beautiful one made of gold above it, the best of practitioners should have them joined together, with their tails touching one another.
Having placed it in an *adhoyantra* apparatus, one should digest iron therein;
by placing it in a heated mortar (*taptakhalvada*), it is produced without a doubt.
In that case, iron possesses six qualities, while gold possesses [many] qualities;
likewise, the milk-tree, the *jārī*, and the *khañjarī* possess a belly-like form.
One should extract their essence and digest iron therein;
one will undoubtedly digest copper upon seeing those two, just as women [behave] when they see a pair.

Then, having caused the mercury to digest the *graha*, one should subsequently cause it to pervade everything; thereupon gold is produced, which is the means for accomplishing virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
In the winter season, six times the amount should be given; previously, the method for killing medicinal herbs was taught.
What else, O auspicious lady, remains? I have explained this to you in brief.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now I shall further explain the preparation of the pill according to the prescribed ritual;
it bestows immortality, the power of moving through the air, the ability to assume such forms, and the power to move upon the earth.
4b) By the power of the auspicious *raseṃdra*, the practitioner accomplishes his goal;
the wise one should digest the *raseṃdra* that has been thoroughly rubbed with the three staffs (*daṇḍatraya*).
Having combined mercury with copper, as well as iron possessing the luster of a fallen vajra, the procedure is carried out as before.
One should cause iron and the other metals to digest one another;
for indeed, diamonds and diamond-like substances dissolve one another.
If one should digest mercury, mica, and iron in equal proportions, once they have been digested,
one should add the killed [metal] and prepare a pill as follows.
Having placed it inside the belly of a crucible, one should heat it in a fire of *tvak* and *iṅguda*;
by that means, a pill (*guṭikā*) is produced which bestows great enjoyment.
She generates good fortune, increases luster and nourishment,
and undoubtedly bestows immortality upon practitioners.
O dear one, by the mere sight of them, he agitates women as well as practitioners;
for six months, O lord of practitioners, he remains within their mouths.
O Goddess of the gods, that which is performed while living likewise bestows a lifespan of ten thousand years;
indeed, the pill called Amarasundarī remains within the mouth for eight months.
5a) In Saṃjīva, one lives for twenty thousand years, free from hunger and disease;
by a gradual increase, the lifespan in [the next hell] is forty thousand years.
And it cannot be pierced by weapons such as discuses, thunderbolts, or mallets;
O Goddess of Sādhanas, it arises as a state of being clinging like a flower.
Even if he is struck by blows from the Vajra-staff and other weapons, or by many bolts of lightning,
that one of great body and great strength is not pierced.
There is no doubt that this occurs through the grace of the pill when it is accomplished by means of the practice, O Goddess, according to the tradition of Kākacaṇḍeśvarī.
Thus ends the Amarasundarī pill.

Now I shall further describe another pill, the "Beautiful One of the Three Worlds" (Trailokyasundarī), O Goddess; as long as it remains in the mouth, one becomes agitated and overwhelmed with passion.
O fair-faced one, by means of her, the three worlds— including the women of the Gaṇas and Gandharvas— would be agitated at the sight of her by the practitioner.
I shall describe in brief the pill known as Trailokyasundarī;
having taken its essence, one attains the splendor of Vajra, Vaiṣṇava, and Vakra.
Having ground together the three metals— gaganam (mica), madanāri (copper), and mahārasa (mercury)—
along with tridaṇḍa, one should treat it with the group of alkaline substances.
When these two have been produced again, one should cast them into the belly of a heated crucible;
once they have been liquefied, O beloved, one should form them into a ball (golaka) in equal proportions.
Having meditated upon that which is fashioned from *vajramuṣā*, one should likewise prepare a pill;
by its name *Trailokyasundarī*, one shall become equal to Kāmadeva.
Thus ends the Trailokyasundarī pill according to the tradition of Kākacaṇḍeśvarī.
Now I shall further describe another pill, the "Deluder of the Three Worlds."
But just as one who is deluded in this world becomes established like a diamond—
if one should pierce even a single [mark] on his face, he shall live for a hundred thousand years.
Possessing the measure of sixteen spans, he is a vajra-body of great strength;
he is born from the arising of Great Passion—of this there is no doubt.
The noble woman is overwhelmed and deluded; there is no doubt that she is like a practitioner who moves at will, with his face bound between the eyebrows.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain how the pill (guṭikā) is produced:
it is Mātaṅgī, Kākacaṇḍā, and Gajamadahāriṇī.
O Dear One, [the goddesses] are Kākī, Kokilā, Kaṅkālī, Vajrā, Vajrā, Trikālikā, Hayamukhī, Naramukhī, Madanāsyā, and likewise Kākatuṇḍā.
The *śukacañcu* is the *nārī*; the *ākula* is the *karapuṭṭaka*. The *mātaṅgī* is the *mātaṅga*, and the *puṣpa* is the *kākajaṅghikā*, known as *kāka*.
"Caṇḍā" refers to a Caṇḍālī woman; "gaja" refers to the frontal globes of an elephant;
"pippilikā" or "pāṭhaka" refers to a cricket; and "kāka" refers to both the crow and the owl.
*Kāme* [is] born of fire, O Goddess; *vajre*, *iti*, *mihuṇḍike*; *vadyati*, *kāmitirikāḥ*; *hayanaradanamarīsyā*.
Thus ends the Caṇḍālī-union.
*Kākatuṇḍā*, *kākāḍīśakrā*, *śukacañcukā*, *umātiśālmalī*, and *kācamācikā* are synonyms for the plant known as *kākamācī*.
Vimeti is indeed Citraka, and Nāḍī is called Nāḍikā;
O Goddess, Madanāntakarī is said to be Haridrā.
With the words "kāmitika hihala pātu ham," [he forms] the hand-gesture of the pericarp;
with the words "añjalayaṭhī karūjuyāl lohidaṇḍa lohitaṃśukam," [he forms] the gesture of the joined palms.
Brahmadaṇḍī is prescribed as the downward-facing flower, and Sahadevikā is the goddess.
6b) A cow’s udder-shaped mark on the chest.
Iśvarī, Aiśvarya, and Madanā—Madanā refers to the madana fruit; and Raparā—these have been briefly described by me as Rasaiḥ and Eva.
O Goddess, the best of practitioners should grind the mercury together with the group of great medicinal herbs (mahoṣadhīgaṇa) and Mātaṅgī flowers for seven days.

By equalizing that with gold, and having made the diamond (*vajra*) and mica (*abhra*) equal to the mercury (*rasa*), the lord of practitioners should grind them; therein a pill is produced which deludes the three worlds—
of gods, asuras, humans, nāgas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
He shall become capable of assuming forms at will and may traverse the three worlds;
freed from all diseases, he shall live for sixty-two years.
He shall become beloved by all women and attain incomparable good fortune;
he shall be invincible to all the gods, possessing a body of adamant and great strength.
There is no doubt in this matter according to the tradition of Kākacaṇḍeśvarī;
now, therefore, O beautiful one, I shall fully explain the *guṭikā* (pill) of victory.
O auspicious lady, the man in whose mouth these remain becomes one with a vajra-body;
namely, vajra, abhraka, the three metals, and that which is almost equal to kāntaloha.
Then one should digest the *rasendra* (mercury), which is *cuṃvaka*, *bhrāmaka*, and *tīkṣṇa*;
first, however, one should rub it with the paste of three medicinal herbs.
O beloved, one should administer it when [the mercury] has been melted and killed, and fashion it into pills;
first, however, one should smear the medicinal herb with the juice of the *triṇīmuṣā* plant.
Having bound it with a pill, one should begin the process of smelting;
then the mercury, having become liquefied, shines with a divine brilliance equal to ten million suns.
Having performed the worship, one should wear it on the mouth; [then] the Vajra-body of great power shall be impenetrable by all weapons, such as swords, discs, mallets, and the like.
Even when being split, he is not pierced, for his body is adamantine;
he is of great heroism, inexhaustible, and likewise immortal.
The lord of practitioners shall indeed become free from old age and disease;
he shall become difficult for all women to resist and capable of assuming any form at will.
"O auspicious one, the victory of the Asuras is invincible even by the gods and Dānavas;
for thus, O Sovereign of Sādhakas, the power of the scripture is indeed accomplished."
"Indeed, since you have asked me about this matter according to the doctrine of Kākacaṇḍeśvarī,
I shall now further describe another [method], the pill that grants the enjoyment of all desires."
7b) Renowned by the name Khecarī and worshipped by gods and gandharvas,
all the deities roam in the great city that is without support.
By the power of the pill, she attained the state of moving through the sky;
therefore, she is called Khecarī, as has been proclaimed in brief.
The wise man should cause the birth-impurity (sūtaka) to be seized and encircled with three threads;
then, being well-composed, he should cast a piece of wood from the Varuṇa tree [into the fire].
Furthermore, the procedure for binding the essence of mercury with cold water is as follows:
when thrown into the water, this [mercury] quickly rises up; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, that man becomes able to assume any form at will and wanders through the three worlds;
he becomes beloved by all women, as well as by the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
It is accomplished here, there is no doubt; according to the tradition of Kākacaṇḍeśvarī.
Now I shall further explain another [practice], the Khecarī which moves through the sky;
it is difficult for all women to attain, how much more so for human beings!
In other scriptures as well, one should establish liberation and its locus through the means;
they say this is "liberation with the physical body" (sapiṇḍa-mukti) according to the Kākacaṇḍeśvarī doctrine.
O beloved, for the benefit of practitioners, I have been asked by you here:
"O auspicious one, how does a lord among practitioners attain the power of traveling through the sky?"
Hayamārī, Kālarātrī, Naramārī, Gajamārikā,
Mamārī, Viśvamārī, Vārāhī, and Aśvamārikā.
Māhiṣa, Viśvamārī, Jalamārī, and Vajrā—
these, in brief, are the secret names of the medicinal herbs.
"Hayā" is Hayacaṇḍālī; "Kākā" is Mṛgacaṇḍikā;
"Gajā" is Gajacaṇḍālī; and "Bhaṃmārī" is Ādityabhaktikā.
O Beloved, she is Naramārī, Caṇḍikāsyā, and also Girikarṇikā;
she is Viśvamārī, Rudrajadyā, Jalamārī, and Dugdhapūyudha.
Vārāhī, mārī, śnuhī, vajrī, mahiṣamāriṇī, and caṇḍī are [names of] these plants;
karkoṭikā is to be known as viṣṇumārī, and kākatiktā [is another].
Jalamārī is said to be fire; it takes away the essence of medicinal herbs.
One should grind mercury (sūtaka) together with [the herb] for seven days in a heated mortar.
One should begin the process of impelling the mercury into the belly of the crucible;
there is no doubt that the lord of mercury (rasendra) will certainly die at that very moment.
Having placed the *śīpra* in the mouth, O Goddess, one traverses the sky in an instant;
freed from old age and death, one wanders through the three worlds.
It is accomplished; there is no doubt here, according to the Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata.
The pill for traveling through the sky.
Now I shall describe another such *khecarī*, said to grant the perfection of the pill (*guṭikā-siddhi*); the mercury (*rasendra*) should be prepared as before.
Having ground it and made it into a pill together with the flowers of the *mātaṅgī*,
one becomes capable of assuming any form at will and, through the power of intense passion, can utterly delude others.
One should fashion a *golaka* (globule) produced from a *brāhmī* maiden,
encased in three metals (*triloha*), and having performed worship according to the prescribed rite.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform a great worship and offer a sacrificial oblation (bali) consisting of great meat combined with fruits of great potency.
When the maiden and the host of yoginīs have satisfied the teacher,
the excellent practitioner should cause the Lord Bhairava Bahuka to recite [the mantra].
Having paid homage and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, unhusked grains, incense, garments, ornaments, and so forth, one should diligently satisfy them all.
Having thrown the pill into his mouth, a man becomes invisible;
he sports with the Guhyakas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, and Śākinīs.
Guarded by Brahmarākṣasas, he sports together with the Kuṣmāṇḍas;
possessing great strength and victory over all, he is invincible even by the hosts of Yoginīs.
Wandering through all the islands,
moving according to her own will, she enjoys divine pleasures together with women who can assume any form at will.
Likewise, O auspicious lady, that excellent practitioner, possessing great power and able to assume any form at will,
becomes as subtle as a shadow and then sports there.
"In this manner, Bhairavī sports with the Guhyakas in the presence of the Lord," according to the Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata.
The illustrious Kākacaṇḍeśvarī said:
O Lord of Gods, for the benefit of practitioners, I ask you about that supreme method which brings about divine accomplishments without difficulty and for the purpose of spiritual attainment.
O Lord of Gods, tell me all that a man performs through action devoid of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), since I am your beloved from the beginning.
The illustrious Omniscient One said:
Listen, O Kākacāmuṇḍā, you who are dear to the extraction of mercury; I shall tell you in brief that which brings benefit to practitioners.
The eight medicinal herbs are as previously described; however, on the left side, they are combined with the juices:
Kāmukī, Vajrakandā, Kaṭukambī, and Rājitā.
One should grind *karkoṭī*, *gṛdhaparṇā*, *kākāṇḍī*, and *vyāghrapādikā* with mercury; when heated, a man [should apply this] to his stomach.
O beloved, one should grind it very firmly with the group of sour substances for seven days;

Having become dead and devoid of processing, it becomes a measure of grain;
it effects a thousandfold transmutation, and thus the great elixir is perfected.
O Goddess, O beloved, hear this from me, the maker of liberation and the maker of gold:

Having prepared the mica, one should perform the killing of mercury for the sake of its medicinal benefit.
One should grind it according to the prescribed rule, combined with the juice of *nṛhatī*;
likewise, the joyful practitioner should grind the mercury for seven days.
Abhra that appears like fresh butter or barley should be placed inside a heated crucible, and one should pour the mercury into its center with it.
Having rubbed mercury with a juice and cast it [into the crucible], one should apply the lower hand;

Having added six times its weight of iron and eight times its weight of gold,
one should coat the interior of the crucible and roast it for one month.
