possessing a great body and great vigor, his lifespan shall be a thousand years.
21a) Or rather, what is the use of much speaking? For those who apply this method according to the rules, it always increases their lifespan and causes them to assume a divine body.
Having cast into the iron vessels kūṣmāṇḍa fruits, various kinds of liquors, other fruits, stones, and abundant foodstuffs;
By consuming milk as food until it is digested, a man shall possess a vajra-body;
he will have a divine body in every respect and shall live for ten thousand years.
By consuming [the substances] with the six syllables and practicing according to the three syllables,
the lord of practitioners becomes one who avoids the faults of passion and aggression, and through that year, he attains a lifespan equal to a kalpa.
The seeds of iṅguḍī and śaila-bhūta, when placed in water,
cause the immobilization of tin by that very means of application.
Water mixed with mercury destroys poison;
when combined with mercury and covered with a coating of wax, it likewise [destroys poison].
One should cast the impurity into the middle of the crucible until it becomes solid;
when a thousandth part of the metal has been pierced through, it shall become gold.
One should take one *pala* of jaggery and one *karṣa* of juice;
having ground these with water, one should place them in a bell-metal vessel.
But when whatever has been thrown into that vessel becomes solid, it should be swallowed with the mouth; this removes all diseases.
One should join the vajra-body with ten times the strength of a nāga in the vital breath;
in the abdomen, after a long time, there is no doubt regarding auspiciousness through this half-measure.
Then, having taken *saṃlohaka*, one should place it within a ram’s horn;
when it has dried thoroughly, that powder becomes excellent.
By that hundredth part of a naga, gold becomes seedless;
in ancient times, the Earth was propitiated by Vusmuṇa and yielded [the gold] from the sun.
That which causes the cessation of one's knowledge and the turning away from the Veda should be known as "mountain-water" (śailodaka), and likewise it becomes "Viṣṇu-sweat."
One should consume ghee and rice, remain constantly devoted to physical exercise,
and perform massage with mountain water as a rejuvenative tonic.
"Immortal, undecaying, possessing a vajra-body, and of great strength"—
thus ends the chapter on Śailodaka according to the Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata.
22a) The illustrious Goddess said:
On the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, I ask Mahādeva, the God of gods and Teacher of the World, about the ritual manual of the Vaitālaka.
For the benefit of practitioners, [this is] the destroyer of death and poverty.
The venerable Īśvara said:
Excellent, excellent, O noble lady! Since you have asked this for the benefit of practitioners, I shall speak that which is difficult to obtain.
O fair-faced one, having washed the realgar with rice-water, O lady of excellent hips,
one should subsequently grind it together with rice grains.
Furthermore, one should cause a ball together with its back to be made of sixty-fold [grain];
having thrown it into the middle of water, it then becomes completely cooled.
Having dried it in the heat of the sun, performed worship,
and ground it into powder, one who is composed should consume it with honey and clarified butter for seven nights.
Resplendent with the hue of the rising sun, possessing his own true form, and pleasing to behold,
he attains the power of moving through the sky, endowed with great strength and prowess.
In the second week, O Goddess, those with the moon on their heads fall;
by that, skin and teeth [are formed], and thus the cavities [of the senses] arise— of this there is no doubt.
The third [form] has seven locks of hair resembling bees;
it possesses the luster of molten gold and has the appearance of a sixteen-year-old youth.
With [the consumption of] conch, kunda, and moon-like flowers, one becomes free from the afflictions of the body;
having attained the strength of nine elephants, one may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
I shall further proclaim the auspicious procedure for *tālaka*.
O Goddess, one takes *tālaka* and grinds the mercury (*sūtaka*) with it.
One should consume one māṣa of this goddess daily, day after day,
until it reaches the measure of one karṣa over twenty-one days.
It destroys even the eighteen types of leprosy that have arisen;
O Siddhikeśvarī, one becomes like the rising sun.
Having attained the lord of the yoga of perfection, he obtains supreme accomplishment;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, he performs oblations for two desired years.
Having become as strong as nine elephants, he lived by means of the moon, sun, and stars;
and having gathered water and wood, he made them into a fire-drill.
Having thoroughly purified the talaka with that clarified butter using a closed crucible,
[one should do so] from the month of Śrāvaṇa until the full moon of Kārttika, for five months.
23a) When it has stood for a period of Puṣkara at the midpoint, one should extract it on an auspicious day;
one should then grind that mercury and consume one māṣa of it.
Having risen early each day for seven days,
on the second week, the hair becomes like a swarm of bees.
Bestowing good fortune, health, and glory, and delighting the hearts of both men and women,
one sports with celestial nymphs through this practice for a single month.
Having thus prepared it with great effort using wood from the Brahmavṛkṣa tree,
one should combine the lock (tālaka) with mercury and administer it together with dhātrī.
That [substance], which is to be processed with buffalo dung, does not become separated from its clear state;
it remains so for twenty-one days until it becomes thoroughly dried.
By consuming this perfected elixir, one will become equal to Bṛhaspati;
conversant with the meaning of various scriptures, one shall be invincible upon the entire earth.
Having combined talaka and mercury, one should grind them together;
one should also grind them with the juice of tālamūlī, mixed with the mercury.
Having rubbed an iron vessel with jambīra wood,
one should take that tālaka and throw it into the jambīra fruits.
23b) When wrapped in the place of a buffalo hide, it attains the state of being free from odor. Again, combined with mercury, one should cook it in the *mātuliṅga* fruit.
One should eat one *māṣa* weight [of the substance] along with betel leaf;
by practicing this for one month, the desired success will be attained.
All metals are colored [into gold] by means of a *puṭa* seal;
thus, in the tradition of Kākacaṇḍeśvarī, the *tālaka-kalpa* (the ritual procedure for orpiment) is completed.
The extraction of the essence of yellow orpiment.
One should grind mercury and realgar together in an iron vessel;
then, one should cover it with the pulp of a citron and a layer of buffalo dung.
One should pierce a single masha-bean through the middle of a betel leaf;
by this practice for one month, one shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
24a) One should grind together mica (abhraka), mercury (rasa), and sulfur (gandhaka) with a three-pronged pestle until it forms a ball (golaka).
The section on the *niṃva* plant.
Having placed it in a vessel made of *picumanda* wood, the practitioner should perform the rite for one year;
he who consumes it for six months shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
One should place the mercury, processed with the three staffs (tridaṇḍa), upon a śālmalī tree;
after one year has passed according to this measure, one should consume it again and again.

And by means of this practice for six months, one may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. Furthermore, I shall now explain another procedure for the preparation of ash-mercury (*bhasmasūta*).
Having ground the juice of *devadālī* together with mercury and sulfur, one should cook it;
the mercury then becomes the ash of *puṭayāka*.
One should consume one *māṣika* [measure] with a betel leaf for a month; by this measure for one fortnight, it cures abdominal diseases, leprosy, and other ailments.
By practicing in this manner, one should consume ten palas;
thus freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one attains great strength and prowess.
One who possesses the vision of gold and is wise shall live for two hundred years;
the prudent one should consume it threefold along with the ash-mercury according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess of the practitioners, she shall live for exactly five hundred years;
thus ends the *Laghusūtaka*.
Oṃ saḥ saḥ, cause to flow, cause to flow; cause the nectar to flow. Oṃ mahau haṃ hasaḥ svāhā! Perform, perform [the extraction of] Soma from the lake. This is the mantra for cutting the Śālmalī tree.
I shall further proclaim another great electuary according to the prescribed rite:
the pungent juice of the *dhātrī* fruit combined with the blood of a night-stalker (*niśācara*) that has been killed by a spear.
He who licks [this] with the three myrobalans (triphalā), honey, and ghee becomes free from old age and death.
[One should take] sulphur, mercury, iron (tīkṣṇa), and tin (kānti).
In the case of equal proportions of *samardhi*, *ārtagala*, and *palāśa* seeds, two types of *tripauṣadha* arise; likewise with *śilājatu* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
One should grind these in equal parts with *arka* and *dhātrī*,
and having heated them with the juice of *taṇḍulīya*, one should further grind them together with *triphalā*.
One should grind [the substance] combined with a decoction of khadira wood and mixed with peacock bile,
according to the prescribed method, along with the juices of the arka plant.
One should place it in a vessel smeared with the juice of triphalā mixed with kanti;
furthermore, one should apply external ointments made from gojihvā and triphalā.
One should place that external coating of clay inside an earthen vessel and bury it in the ground at the depth of a knee, using the *puṭa* method.
25b) Clay, plaster, and cow dung should be applied from top to bottom;
likewise, perfumes and incense should be offered daily for one full year.
Having performed worship and having extracted [the substance], one should worship the gods and the Brahmins;
one should consume that great delicacy combined with honey and clarified butter.
On auspicious days, under favorable constellations, when the moon is bright and the planetary positions are excellent,
the destruction of leprosy occurs on the first and seventh [days].
Completely freed from all diseases, having attained the great essence (mahārasa) the size of a grain of kanaka,
one becomes the imperishable Khecarī at every seventh stage.
This very elixir does not succeed for one who possesses little merit;
nor is mercury produced without *kānta* iron, nor is *kānta* iron found devoid of mercury.
It does not migrate into the body, nor into the mass of food, like [a reflection] into water.
Thus ends the procedure for the Great Elixir (*mahārasāyaṇa*).
26a) Oṃ, homage to Rasendra!
Relying upon Dharma and fame, this compendium of aesthetic flavors (rasas) is being told;
for without the constituent substances (dravyas), [the flavors] do not succeed, therefore follows the description of the substances.
Victorious is Rasavarendra, the destroyer of diseases such as leprosy and skin eruptions;
it strikes down all these ailments, and the wrinkles and grey hair of men perish.
It bestows long life, delicious food, and the power of moving through the sky.
When one has mastered the eighteenth essence of action (karmarasa),
it destroys his old age, death, poverty, and even death itself.
From sweating comes vision; by reviving the fainting state, the upward breath is restrained;
through restraint comes kindling, according to the measure of the "swallowing of space."
The procedure for churning and the method of sublimation,
as well as the subsequent internal messenger, the alkaline flux, and the digestion for the purpose of coloring.
Killing and likewise piercing—these indeed are eighteen in sequence.
There is no accomplishment through sweat, nor through fire, nor even through the cultivation of the left-hand path;
sweat is merely a variety of liberation, while the eight karmas shall now be explained.
The procedure for the application of sweating, digestion (*jāraṇa*), and killing (*māraṇa*);
indeed, digestion is to be understood as the eightfold action.

One who has not reached the end of perspiration does not complete the vow; one who is not impassioned cannot color another; one who is not heated does not become a pond, nor does he even enter into union.
By these ritual procedures, having brought the fire under control, one should offer oblations;
this destroys old age, death, and poverty, and brings about the destruction of suffering.
One should accomplish it through mantras and yantras, by means of the procedure involving sound and the application of fomentation; thus, at that very moment, one binds the mercury (sūtaka).
27a) When it has become smoke-colored, as well as when it is like a frog or a caterpillar,
and likewise during trembling and the kumbhaka [retention]— such is the fivefold movement of the vital essence (rasa).
The procedure for sudation (svedana) will now be described; listen to that which bestows the accomplishment of all combined [therapies]: pāṭhā, punarnavā, elā, aṅgārī, and vicitraka.
Then, having prepared the five medicinal herbs beginning with *devadālī*,
one should cook *sīgru*, *siṃdhava*, and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) in a pot over a swinging fire (*dolāgni*).
One should seal it again; this state of being "dead" is called *jāraṇā*. Cow’s milk and the fruit of the *bījapūraka* are the causes.
Sour jambīra fruit, vetasa, śyāmā, bṛhatī,
and yavaciñcā, along with the leaves of śigru and rock salt in equal proportions, should be cooked together.
Saurāṣṭra, hayakāsīsa, and sindhu,
when combined with sour gruel (āranāla) for twelve days, are said to be called madirārasa.
27b) One should repeatedly perform the impregnation (*bhāvanā*) of mica powder many times in a well-heated iron mortar (*loha-khalva*), together with *siṃdhunā* (rock salt).
When the *sūtaka* (mercury) and *cābhraka* (mica) become a globule (*golaka*) within [the crucible],
there is the process of gold-making with excellent golds, and the process of silver-making with excellent silvers, and so forth.
Having prepared a crucible, one should blow upon it and grind the mica-ore;
then, by means of the "secret transmission" (*saṃketacāraṇa*), [the mercury] should be processed in double or triple quantities of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*).
And I shall proclaim the process of digestion (jāraṇa), which is the conduct of the mercury's meal;
one should effect this digestion by means of these substances, including sindhu, vidrā, and anvitta.
One should apply sudation; at the moment of conjunction, it binds the mercury and causes it to undergo transformation.
Now we shall explain another [method].

One should fill a crucible in the shape of a cow’s udder with a globule of mercury and mica, having arranged it with openings at the bottom and top, and then pour in the liquid while it is heated by the sun.
28a) One should cause it to be melted below by means of a mild fire.
One should give a very small amount of mercury, a very small amount of camphor, sour substance, and sea salt;
thus, when [the mercury] has been digested over three days, the process of assimilation (jāraṇa) and so forth begins with the consumption of morsels (grāsa).
There are three signs of being worn out, and the fourth is that it has become like a lump of clay. Now follows the procedure for diamond (*vajra*) and *vaikrānta*.
When *ṭaṅkaṇa* is struck with the application of a divine medicinal herb, its surface becomes smooth;
at that very moment, the mercury is bound, as is the essence of mica (*abhraka-rasa*) in the aforementioned operations.
Thus ends the process of digestion (jāraṇa).
Now, the liquefaction.

Hingu, ashṭakaṇa, and savya—these three combined together constitute the excellent digestion and assimilation of mercury; O beloved, these are the eight mercurial processes (rasas) that are always pleasing.
Now we shall provide the explanation.
28b) A conch shell powdered with the milk of the *arka* plant is highly esteemed;
this alone is the best *viḍa* salt, the supreme for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury.
The substance named Guḍa is prepared by repeatedly processing ash with strained cow’s urine until it has acquired the nature of sulphur.
Now we shall explain.
A leaf-packet made of radish tubers should be burnt; the resulting ash is strained with cow's urine.
With that, the sulphur should be processed one hundred times, repeatedly.
Thus has been described the best method for purifying sulfur;
alternatively, it may be strained through cow's urine after being mixed with citraka-water and ashes.
But that which is joined with many meditations is called the supreme knowledge;
it is strained through cow's urine and filtered by the juices of *lakṣaṇa*, *kṣāra*, and *parasa*.
One should cause the patient to drink this *āmrājiṇī* preparation as prescribed; it should be taken with sea salt, rock salt, and *sauvarcala* salt.
29a) Vidula also recommends this.
Combine one thousand parts each of javakṣāra, sauvarjika, and ṭaṅkaṇa;
along with the alkalis of mekṣaka, kapāla, and asana, and the alkalis of sesame and apāmārga.
One should strain the impure [substance] through a cloth using cow’s urine, along with *vajrakṣāra*, *arkakṣāra*, castor seeds, *unmatta*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa*.
This is indeed the best method for dissolving all metals:
take two parts each of turmeric, madder, pataṅga, and red sandalwood.
Take equal parts of kusuṃbha, kuṅkuma, and haṃsapāda,
along with ṭaṅkaṇa, mākṣika, śaṅkha, and white glass.
When applied with a counter-remedy, the impurities of the talaka and the jīva are removed;
it becomes pure silver, the most excellent wealth of fame.
O Goddess, for one whose body is like a cloud free from obstruction, the seventeenth [digit] is sixteenfold; and the third is indeed crooked, piercing through more than a hundred peaks.
One should cause the essence (sattva) of tāra (silver), mṛtavaṅga (dead tin), and śvetābhraka (white mica) to flow out; one should collect that which flows out.
Thus, when seven cycles have been completed until only the stars remain,
it becomes distinct from the sixteen [parts] and is melted by a quarter portion.
The hundredfold piercing (śatavedha) should be performed as before, once the union of the seed-syllables (bīja-melana) has been understood. Thus it is said.
I shall now describe the process of coloring, according to the procedure for white and yellow;
I will explain the method of extraction and the causal agent when [the substances] are mixed with cow's ghee and buffalo's ghee.
It should be prepared with the meat of iguana, rabbit, and goat, along with red and yellow pigments, boiled in resin and sesame oil; that shall be the *sā* [preparation].
One should accomplish the application for the purpose of extraction in the process of mercury;
[this involves] *haradantī* equal to the semen, processed with oil over fire for seven days.
In this manner, there is a remedy for the act of recollection:
take mercury (hara), lead (pārada), dantī, and the seeds of samaṅkā in equal parts.
One should take the seeds of *vīja* (Cannabis sativa), the seeds of *harī* (Terminalia chebula), and indeed the seeds of *tāra* (Euphorbia tirucalli);
these should be combined in equal parts, with one part of *tāra* and one part of *nāga* (Mesua ferrea).
Place the fire below and prepare it with oil;
one should place ten crucibles there, each containing ten flowers.
One part of mercury seed (hemabīja) should be treated with *āvarta* [mercury];
thus, one should rub that which has become a body of equalized essence (*samarasa*).
The casting down of the sentient being (satvapātana) will now be explained.
Having taken equal portions of powdered *guggulu*, black earth,
and *kavalā* (myrobalan), these should be boiled in milk.
At the time of digestion, having added mica (abhraka), stir it and make it well-mixed;
having formed a pill with that, one should digest it for seven days.
And when the mineral essence of mica has fallen into a fire of acacia wood embers,
that is another formulation.
One should mix the cloud-powder for seven or ten days;
then, having obtained it from the midst of the *ca calva* and *sapiṇḍa*, perform the heating for the duration of those days.
And soft śīśaka ore, as well as abhraka ore, constantly falls [as dross];
likewise mākṣika ore.
One suffering from fresh fever should take honey with Gandharva-taila and ghee; or likewise, one should eat a bolus (vaṭī) prepared with Vārtāka and fermented gruel (bhūṣa).
One should perform the saturation of honey combined with plantain juice;
likewise, one should cast the honey into a crucible that has been heated.
31a) Truth is like the lord of serpents, and likewise, movement is like a deer;
and that which has the brilliance of fire is indeed the essence of honey.
*Drājau* is known as *dreti*; *gandharvati* belongs to the two *erāvayas*.
*Vātavatī* is to be known from *lakṣmaṇā*, and *avadeti* refers to *kumārīgandhaka*.
One should smear that beloved of Varāha with betel leaves and bell-metal;
by this very practice, performed at the three junctions of the day, one becomes possessed of yoga.
The six classes of beings fall together like a single flock of birds;
now follows another yoga.
One should grind kaṅkuṣṭha and ṭaṅkaṇa with the milk of a woman;
when thrown into a heated crucible, it falls down even in the absence of a cover.
One should grind together seven *guñjā* seeds with the impurity from the ear of a female buffalo and the impurity from the ear of a donkey.
31b) A coating of kaṅkuṣṭha, ṭaṅkaṇa, breast milk, or mica is cast upon the heated [metal] in a crucible;
this is the flux for smelting.
Even a woman, having processed castor oil with the milk of the *vajrī* plant, should fumigate it along with her hair; [the resulting substance] will fall upon the ores of copper and iron.
The powder of the mineral (tāpya) and mercury are both restless by their very nature;
how then can mercury be bound upon the earth?
In another reading:

Iron is softened by fermented rice-water (āranāla) and heated with alkaline salt; then, having been rubbed together with ghee and honey, it becomes a "woman's thunderbolt" (strīravajraka) when smelted.
Having treated it with an alkaline substance, together with ghee and honey,
and having added soot from a house-fire, one should blow upon it to extract its essence.
Having indeed made the gold into a single mass, it becomes fallen;
having held it with one-eighth part, perform the union with the essence (sattva).
The method for extracting the essence of iron ore (sūta) and copper ore (mititāpya),
as well as the method for the essence of orpiment (tālaka).
Having made the mercury and the mica (rasatāla) equal in measure, one should grind them with pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa);
one should place the mixture in a crucible and cover it with a copper vessel.
Indeed, for two watches (six hours) after the completion of Śaktikāpūrī,
once it has been made cool, the essence of the palm (tālasattva) is prepared.
In this manner, by means of the application of the prescribed method, the extraction of the essence (*sattva*) from both *kuṣṭha* and mercury is achieved using sulfur and an iron vessel.
The method for extracting the essence of yellow orpiment.
Thus ends the procedure for the precipitation of mercury, from the *Śrīrasasārottara*, in the dialogue between Caṇḍī and Maheśvara.
I shall describe the killing of metals according to their order, like a host of enemies: tin by means of brass, lead by realgar, iron by mica, and mercury by orpiment and stone.
One should destroy bell-metal with gandha, copper with that same substance, and silver with the juice of mākṣika.
Thus ends the section on the slaying of the host of enemies.

[The mercury] is mounted upon *haritāla*, made into a paste with equal parts, saturated, and treated six times with fragrant [substances]. Thus, having been killed three times, it becomes truly liquefied; this great essence (*mahārasa*) penetrates both the Moon and the Sun. *Commentary:* "Hara" refers to mercury (*pārada*); "pannaga" refers to lead (*nāga*); "Garuḍa" refers to the seed of gold (*hemabīja*). Having taken these in equal portions (*sama*),...
It is made uniform in consistency by means of a mild fire over a bed of oil. It should be held with oil in a strong bell-metal vessel until it flows; thus one should digest the remaining mercury.
33a) The previously mentioned procedure for killing [the enemy]; the great elixir that pierces the moon and the sun.
Mounted upon Garuḍa, three-eyed, with a soft, inner white complexion,
one traverses a hundred thousand yojanas in the vulva-like expanse of the earth, which is as firm as sulfur.
Commentary.
Having ascended the battle of the three eyes and the three rasas, one should take the seed of gold (hemabīja), soft and lovely, very soft, and lead (sīsaka).

With a leaf of the *kāṅkānti* plant, these two should be prepared; over the heat of six fires, one should apply the powder of sulfur and honey, which has been infused with female flower-essence (*strīpuṣpa*). This should be given as a counter-additive (*pratīvāpa*) and maintained.
One should digest it until ten parts remain, then triple it according to the previously mentioned method of killing.
One should kill that [metal] three times; now I shall describe the purification of metals according to the procedure for *śulva*, as well as the preparation of *gandhaka*.
Having melted it with castor oil and *araṇī* oil, one should place it in a clay crucible.

Then, having applied [the powder] to a paste of *Dhattūra* juice, one should perform gentle fomentation with goat’s milk for one day. Then, one should saturate *Abhayā* seven times with a mixture of *Rāsnā* and *Madhu*. Thus it is said.

Purification of Sulphur (Gandhaka): Sulphur should be cooked in oil with cow’s bile (*gopitta*) and buffalo buttermilk (*mahiṣītakra*) in a *dolāyantra* for three days. Then, having placed it in a small pouch (*poṭalikā*) inside a citron (*bījapūraka*), one should cook it over a mild fire. This should be done three times, followed by [treatment] with peacock bile and the juice of *palāśa*. Thus ends the purification of cinnabar (*darada*). [Now follows] the purification of realgar (*śilā*).
Having heated realgar many times with cow-bile, with the juice of the ripe citron, and also mixed with the juice of the *vibhītaka*,
this is the purification of realgar.
34a) One should prepare three *puṭas* by thoroughly coating an *arka* leaf with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) saturated with the juice of *dhātrī*,
and then roasting it three times; this should be done repeatedly after drying it with the urine of a calf.

Having ground it and treated it with the juice of betel leaves (*tāmbūlapatra*), one should again perform *puṭapāka* in the same manner. Then, having bound it in a cradle (*dolikā*) with the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and having performed the "breaking of rice" (*taṇḍulabheda*), one should cook it many times. This is the preparation of *tāla*.
One should then boil honey (*mākṣika*) sequentially with sour gruel (*āranāla*), cow urine, and goat urine.

Having processed *kulattha* beans, sour gruel (*āranāla*), and the two types of *kaṣāya* with *kājīra*, one should boil them with the juice of *rājakośātakī* and the juice of the *kūṣmāṇḍagaṇayāri*. Thus is the purification of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). Having prepared rice-water, one should cook it with castor oil (*eraṇḍataila*).
34b) Purification by means of red ochre.
Thus, according to the Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata, [this is] all.
I shall also declare the arrival of benefits for those of the castes beginning with the Ṛṣas;
for the elders, it is threefold, and for the younger ones, it is three times the amount of the *puṭa*.
Taking the paste, taking silver again and again, and taking gold.
Commentary:
*Yām* refers to mercury (*pārada*); *him* refers to cinnabar (*hiṅgula*); *tām* refers to copper (*tātha*).

*Mākṣīkāṅga* refers to sulfur (*gandhaka*). *Ma* refers to realgar (*manaḥśilā*). These are to be taken in increasing order; "increase" means they are to be processed with the juice of *bījapūraka*, or with the juice of *jaṃvīraka* for the smallest dose.
Having made a leaf-cup from pure copper and smeared it with a paste, one should obtain a powder by means of *puṭapāka*.
Then, one should prepare a bolus (*modaka*) of soft powder mixed with equal parts of mercury and ghee; taking three times as much silver, one should thereby produce gold.
35a) When the extraction has been completed in due time, one should add gold-seed (*hemabīja*) equal to one-tenth of the mercury, having recognized the union (*melaka*).
One should also mix an equal amount of processed copper (*śulva*) with it; [mix] the copper powder with cow’s ghee.

When four parts of *modita* have been thoroughly processed with *tāra* (silver), half of that amount is the *kalyāṇaka* alloy (*śulva*). This is not to be processed with the previously mentioned paste. That powder, when mixed with cow’s ghee, should be given along with gold; [the dose is] three *palas*.
One should cause the *triphalā* and *ṣaḍyala* to be processed to the measure of the waist; thus, a fourfold excellence of color occurs.
Alternatively, one should cause it to be processed three times; that same [substance], along with the previously mentioned powdered *mṛtāśulva* and *darada*, [is used].

Equal parts of cow’s ghee and half that amount of *kalyāṇaka* [are used]. Commentary: One part of mercury (*rasa*) and one part of *tālaka* are ground together with the juice of *peṭhaka* for three days. Afterwards, having formed a pill (*tugolaka*), it is placed inside a crucible (*haṇḍikā*).
Having placed a mass of *vajra* [minerals] on top and then covered it with a lid (*sarāva*), [the process continues].

It should be filled with sand and smeared on the upper and lower surfaces; having poured water through the upper opening, one should again place a shallow bowl-seal over it and ignite a fire below. After three *praharas*, when it has cooled to the touch of one's own body, the bronze vessel from above should be taken. Having prepared it, it should be applied to the site of the disorder at the appropriate time. Thus [ends the section]. 4.
The Chapter on Leaves from the *Rasasārottara*:

Take one part of pārābha, two parts of cinnabar (hiṅgula), three parts of gold-māṣī, four parts of sulfur (gandhaka), and five parts of realgar (manaḥśilā); grind them together with the juice of *dhattūra*.

One should prepare a leaf-piercing tool (*kaṇṭakavedhī*) from fifteen parts of purified copper (*śulva*) mixed with lac juice and *kadūta* juice; one should coat it with that. Then, having added a little sulfur (*gandhaka*), one should rub it.
One-fourth part of blue vitriol (*nīlaka*) should be added, and purified borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) should be added in three parts of purified copper.

One part of pure silver should be held in a mūṣikā crucible; one should observe it until it becomes cool like the moon. One should carry out this procedure three times in this manner. In an open crucible, once the silver remains as a residue, the primary seed (ādivīja) should be added in a quantity equal to one-tenth of the silver; this is the method for making silver.

The pericarp of the lotus should be made of copper combined with pure lead; this is the killing of all metals. When [the metal] is refined and marked with a quarter-part [of the additive], it shall become ten-carat gold. Gold and silver [are processed] with the juice of the *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd.

One should grind [the substance] with the milk of *arka*; one should smear the leaves of tin (*vaṅga*), and it dies by means of a *puṭa* (roasting). One should grind *acaṃmuṇḍī* and the juice of *bheda* on a stone slab; one should smear the leaves of lead (*nāga*), and it dies by means of a *puṭa*. It becomes iron (*āyasa*).
One should grind tāpyaka and gandhaka together with goat's milk.
One should coat the copper sheets; thus the copper becomes excellent. Furthermore, one should grind sulfur and realgar with the milk of the *arka* plant.
One should smear it upon silver leaves; a coating (vala) is produced. One should diligently grind the coating of *tāpya* with the decoction of *kāñcanī*.
One should smear it upon gold leaf; the crucible dies in an instant,
like the moon joined with its crescent or the sun with its solar portion.
Two parts of gold, one part each of silver and copper, along with cinnabar, sulfur, mica, and iron pyrite, combined with mercury;

Having placed two parts of the mercury (rasaka) in a mortar, one should grind it for three days; then, using a leaf smeared with the sun and moon (mercury and sulfur), one should rub it in the middle.
The paste of the *varti* pills should be cooked over a mild fire until it becomes soft;
however, for those who do not consume them, this preparation is not required.
First, devotion to Vittala is an elixir for the attainment of both enjoyment and liberation;
yet, one who is deluded by the body does not know this, being most sinful.
I shall describe the purification of metals, which destroys all defects;
by the mere act of purifying them, stainlessness is produced.
37b) [The ore] that is excessively covered by a crust, difficult to melt, and hard to combine— when impure, all such metals perish through the six defects.
Just as a pure field yields grain,
so too does pure metal manifest its true substance.
First is the purification of the metal, and the field is the second;
third is the transmutation by mercury, and the fourth is the purification of the substance.
One should place the subsequent primary seed-syllable at the beginning and the penetrator of the six (rasa) and the four (veda) in the middle—
the penetrator of the syllables and the non-syllables.
One who knows the final union (melāpaka) at all times destroys all evil;
by beholding the union of Hara and Gaurī, one's sin is utterly destroyed.
Those devoid of merit do not behold this union with the Far Shore.
What is the use of elephants, horses, women, the earth, or hoards of wealth?
Even then, they desire enjoyment as long as the virtuous body remains.
Having attained a human birth, which is difficult for all living beings to obtain,
one should indeed accomplish the elixir of mercury (pārada) by which the self is liberated.
Those evil-minded ones who defile their guru and the deity with a wicked soul fall into a terrible hell, from which there is no return for them.
In the sky, the number of zodiac signs is likewise five hundred;
this is the examination of mica (abhraka).
White, yellow, likewise red, and black as well as another; for each color, one should prepare twice the amount.
He knows that there are four kinds of abhraka for practitioners:
the white is to be known as Brāhmaṇa, and those of red color as Kṣatriya.
The Vaiśyas are declared to be yellow, and the Śūdra is said to be black; furthermore,
for each individual caste, there are four types of birth.
One should perform the examination using Pinākī, Dardurī, Vajrī, and Raseśvara as the fourth; then one may commence the ritual action.
Having placed it in the midst of milk, one should cook it over a gentle fire;
the wise person should continue cooking it until the milk is released [from the vessel].
Then, having placed it in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), one should heat it again and again;
[the substance] should be taken from the crucible while it is still warm into milk or water.
One should have the examination of that great abhraka performed there;
it should produce a "taṭataṭa" sound, and its bark-like layer appears everywhere.
One should know Rasendrī as the most excellent in the matter of alchemical operations;
she also increases one's vigor, and thus she is known as Pinākī.
That which is heated and indestructible like a frog is called *dardurī*;
that which has the form of a thunderbolt (*vajra*) is called *vajrī*.
Even the wielder of the Pināka bow attains length when the short vowel 'u' is employed in the act of marking;
even a frog becomes large when it is seen by a frog-catcher.
O Goddess, by means of the vajra created by the Vajrin, one is born with a vajra-body;
it is proclaimed to be fourfold, established according to its nature.
Īśvara said:
Just as devotion becomes firm through the teacher's guidance, so too,
by the grace of the guru’s feet, one may outwit the terrible time of death.
Having sprinkled water on the face, the sign there is as follows:
O Goddess, one should predict life by warmth and death by coldness.
Just as water that has become cold leads to death after six months, so too shall there be destruction throughout all the worlds; listen to the cause of this action, O fair-faced one.
When the garden moves, the wind blows upward;
one enters the path of death, and likewise experiences death.
When such a sign has arisen, death will certainly occur;
O lady of beautiful hips, by making [the victim] naked, they have fallen under the power of death.
Having performed this, O Goddess of gods, humans afflicted by time (death) should place a gold coin upon a plantain leaf and deposit it there.
O Lord of Gods, the semen falls upon the leaf of a plantain tree;
that semen is mixed with honey and combined with cow’s clarified butter.
O lady of excellent limbs, one should administer a nasal drop (nasya) by which those who have fallen under the power of death are revived;
O lady of excellent limbs, this should be done after blowing [the powder] within the scope of two ghaṭikās.
40a) O Lord of Gods, he may live again through yoga in the abode of Yama;
one should cause the wind to be delivered to him by means of a hollowed-out vessel at whatever place he has gone.
By the grace of the Supreme Lord, she obtained the name Mṛtyusañjīvanī;
indeed, by her, death was brought back to life for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
One should pass the time according to these various distinctions when it has arrived:
[dealing with one] who is hostile toward others, most greedy, engaged in sinful deeds, and corrupted.
O Goddess praised by heroes, one who is endowed with devotion performs that which is beyond description for those released from the nature of worldly existence;
this is the path spoken of by the pure.
And may he, free from the illusion of the highest ignorance, grant to all the world the common food and clothing.
Through right conduct, one shall gradually attain perfection, beginning with the knowledge of Brahman;
O Goddess, when the teacher has been worshipped according to one's means.
O lady of excellent hips, O beautiful as an immortal, I shall tell you the ritual manual by which a yogin attains immortality, O fair-faced one.
There should be five parts of seed, three parts of ghee, and twice that amount of honey; these should be mixed together with Viṣṇu.
O beautiful lady, O excellent woman, one should administer the nasal medication through the left nostril;
he who takes this nasal medication for one month at the time of dawn [attains the desired result].
O beautiful goddess, success shall come to him within a single kalpa;
O lady of excellent hips, the yogi should administer it as a nasal drop for two months.
One who recites the scriptures will become a poet by themselves; O Goddess of the Asuras, such a knower of yoga destroys all diseases entirely.
When the seventh month has arrived for the yogins,
and even for those who have not seen the yogins, through that [attainment] their activity proceeds.
O fair-faced one, by the application of the *dharāmāyā* mantra, one may attain immortality;
likewise, [one attains it] through the union with the *śakti* known as *kuṇḍagolaka*.
O fair-faced one, one should diligently rub it with that [substance] and administer it as nasal medicine;
by practicing this for seven nights, immortality is certainly attained.
Oṃ, homage to Gaṇapati.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for preparing camphor:
one should collect the flowers of the *raṃbhā* plant and cut off their tips.
One should take the nectar of the *raṃbhā* flower and hold it for the measure of a staff;
therein, O Goddess, one should offer the supreme *viṣṇupāṇika*.
Having wrapped it with thread and secured it firmly with a binding— this,
in brief, is the excellent method for preparing camphor.
One should perform [the rite] starting from Caitra until the range of Āṣāḍha;
when the tree is endowed with saplessness, it should be uprooted, O beloved of Pāṇika.
When there is a desire to prepare an edible preparation, one should wash the finest camphor with goat’s milk and then wear it while remaining in a state of well-being.
Then, having dried it in the shade, one should store it in a camphor vessel;
O Goddess of the Gods, that camphor is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds.
Thus ends the preparation of camphor.
O Goddess, for another curiosity, one should grind excellent camphor oil with the tips of *jātī* leaves and *sarjarasa*.
O Queen of the Gods, one should prepare the *kakarāga* with sesame oil;
O Queen of the Gods, the wise practitioner should cook it with an iron rod.
42a) One should pour fully ripened oil into that [vessel] and add camphor;
one should store it in a camphor vessel using a portion of camphor equal to the portion of oil.
That oil is suitable for the deities; one should rub it upon the Gandharvas.
Having taken up the weapons, one should perform the movements of Aḍikā and the gestures of the elephant.
In this manner, one should place the bark inside a vessel (*haṇḍikā*) and then fill that vessel with half a *pāṇi* measure of oil;
having done so, one should seal the opening with a cloth. Alternatively, one should pour water into a ladle (*vāṭukī*) and hold it over the [oil-filled] vessel;
[this is called] the *vāṭukī*.
Having held it above and covered it with that cloth, one should again apply *ḍhakaṇī* on top; this is what was stated above. Thus ends the section on camphor-oil (*karpūrataila*).
42b) One should grind camphor with water on a stone slab using a pestle; one should take its powder and, having filled a tube with water, place a plantain leaf at the opening. (Plantain leaf.)

One should wrap it. Again, one should wrap it with a cloth and bake it in a fire using cow dung as fuel. One should take that powder and place camphor water into its center; it becomes a beautiful *vīṇaka*.
In the case of *pātālaka*, however, one should apply the skin of a *kīta* and cover it with cloth seven times; when the surface is not dried and is heated by fire, it is accomplished.

"Again, for half a watch," it is said; "having taken [the medicine] after opening [the vessel]" means he takes it. And because he maintains a strict regimen, he should again take the *aṇḍī*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *cīrī*, *siṣāḍha*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* separately, one by one. Thus...

Three *pala* of resin (*rāla*), two *madana* fruits, and *aṇḍīcūla* should be placed on top; oil should be poured over them, and another [substance] should be thrown in. One should place three *naṣamūtala* jars inside a crucible (*hāḍī*) and seal it. Another *kūvuḍalī* should be prepared and placed inside; in this way, one should heat the *madana* fruit and resin together until they are fused into one.
Once it has been removed from the fire, it should be taken while still warm from its own heat and not allowed to touch the ground;

then one should add *kūvuḍalī* (2) ground and mix it in. One should apply *aṇḍītvacā* (eggshell), *avaṣidhāryā* (3 ṭaṅkas), *ilā* (3), *cīṭaka* (3), *logaṭaṅkatīnajā* (3), and *phala* (fruit)—all these together—grinding them into a paste.
Having made a fine powder, one should place two *māṣas* of camphor along with fragrant substances inside a vessel;
having perfumed it with a single leaf, the wise person should know [the result]. Thus it is said in the *Uttarādhyayana*.

Take one *ṭaṅka* of *puṣpasevatī* or any fragrant substance that has been crushed; wear it for four *praharas*. When those flowers have faded, another should be applied. In this manner, it must be done daily, and the flowers should be worn for seven days; thus the preparation of the mixed-fragrance powder is accomplished.

Having adorned it all with fine [powder] and prepared everything, one should first place the primary mandala in the center; subsequently, another should be placed. Fragrant flowers should be offered—offered gently during each of the four watches—and likewise on other days. Thus, according to the ritual, for three days one should maintain the small jar (*kūpikā*).

44a) [The preparation] beginning with barley is accomplished, and not otherwise. Thus ends the procedure for barley and the like. Now follows the preparation of musk: one should grind equal parts of black agallochum, nutmeg, saffron, and filaments together.
Having made a fine wick with the juice of *śigru* and *sūla*, one should smear it with *ketakī* leaf. After a single moment, it becomes musk (*kasturikā*).

The powder of the kernel of the *aṃcakī* fruit, cooked and repeatedly processed with the juice of *aṃba*, should then be subjected to *puṭapāka* (sealed heating) many times; thereafter, [add] 1 part *ilā* (cardamom), 2 parts *icī* (spikenard), 3 parts *taja* (star anise), 4 parts *jāvatrī* (nutmeg), 5 parts *kuṭu* (costus), and 6 parts *jāiphala* (nutmeg).

Furthermore, having ground it finely with its accompanying ingredients, one should rub it repeatedly with *ambara* juice; after being infused with camphor water, it becomes musk. Half a *dala* [of this] is white and provides fragrance everywhere.
Having taken [the ingredients] and performed an equal-part blending with the substance, burn *guṇṭhalī*;

that very substance is then blended equally. Again, having placed them together, rub them with *poyasa* oil; it becomes musk (*kastūrikā*). Thus, it becomes smooth and fragrant. Another [method]: [use] old *śrīphala*.
The burden is ungraspable. Its cultivation: 3. Cultivation of fragrant rice with water; 4.

This [is done] in cow urine for one watch (prahara); 3. Cultivation; 5. Having placed the urine of forest-dwellers and householders into a water-vessel, its cultivation in that water is performed three times;
6. Cultivation of hair with water three times; 7. Cultivation of all wood with fragrant water. Now...
The preparation for *dutipātana* should be administered. The preparation with water from *kuṭuka*, *cūrṇata*, and *jāpatra* is to be done separately.

Having tied a knot at the top of the *suramā* plant, and having placed a ball (*piṇḍa*) made of *ilāicī* and *jāiphala*, one should cook this fragrant oil infused with camphor and saffron. Afterwards, having added the ball and water from the *ketakī* flower and *suhaṃjaṇā*, it should be kept in the heat until it becomes liquid; [then] within its shade—

The musk used by one who practices meditation becomes [perfected]. Having ground five *pala* of nails with oil until they turn smoky-colored, one should thereafter grind a stone and bring the root of the *kelī* plant. Having washed it thoroughly, one should place nine *sarāvī* measures of water into a vessel;
having washed the excellent [root] twenty-eight times, that water from the nail [is ready for use].

One should cause [the following] to be infused: five *ṭaṅkas* of *ilāicī*, five *ṭaṅkas* of *tajaṭa*, five *ṭaṅkas* of *nāgakeśara*, five *ṭaṅkas* of *jāiphala*, and five *ṭaṅkas* of *vāḍivandhaṇa*. These should each be taken separately with water.

The contemplation on the desire for clothing (kapaṭaicchā-bhāvanā) is the seventh; it becomes a bestower of success. One should cause five eggs to be offered by means of the fire of the lamp of body-hair.

Then, one should pluck out the hair. When the fire has blazed up, one should offer a beneficial root-tuber and cast water [upon it]. Thereafter, that which remains of the root-tuber should be held. Then, after that, the five eggs and the splinters should be held, and water [should be poured].

One should kindle a fine fire with clarified butter (*paṇīdeya*). Therein, one should place the *aṇḍī* (egg-shaped vessel) into a shallow bowl (*kaṭoraka*) and constantly grind it within the middle of the *syadala*. Again, the *aṇḍī* should be finely filtered through separate pieces of cloth, and the infusion (*bhāvanā*) should be administered; thus it becomes the perfected *siddhidala*.
46a) Bring five eggs and do not cook them over a fire of wool.
Then, when the wool has been torn away, place those eggs in a vessel and pour water into it. Thereafter, a filter is held above; in that filter, there are five eggs.

The *salākā* (measuring stick) should be held and the *āṣāriḍhakaṇī* should be given; one should ignite a fine fire. There, the *aṇḍī* (egg-shaped vessel), being heated, falls into the *kaṭoraka* (bowl); one should grind all that [substance] within its petals. Then, one should grind the *aṇḍī* finely. Into that, one should add the seed (*bīja*) filled with black lute-strings (*kṛṣṇavīṇī*). It is fragrant and excellent.
Thus it is; this is the best musk.
Having squeezed it out using a cloth made of curd, one should cause it to dry in the shade;
then, having prepared it again, it should be infused with musk liquid for another turn.
46b) One should perform a saturation with *alaktārasa* (lac-resin), and with the eighteenth [ingredient] one should give saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and perform a saturation with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*).
Thus the saffron becomes fit for use. One should grind together five parts of *mura*-flesh, five parts of leaf-born [resin], and five parts of pungent oil.

One should cause the *chāyā* (dried extract) to be dried. Having applied the *bhāvanā* (saturation) of *ketakī*, *druti*, *puṭaka*, *maṇḍatikā*, and having added one seed (*vīja*) each, it becomes saffron (*kuṅkuma*). By means of the milk of *kasūbha*, *vīlu*, and *giri*, and after the *bhāvanā* of *pippalī* and lac (*lākṣā*), having added the seed in three parts, it becomes saffron. [This remains effective for] three years.

By the method of washing turmeric with *akṣa* (Vibhītaka) and the bark of *sigru*, it becomes as white as a jasmine flower; when mixed with sour gruel (*amlakāñjika*), it dies away [loses its color]. Then, having ground it again with milk and performed an infusion (*bhāvanā*) with *alaṭā*, adding one-third part of seed (*bīja*), it becomes saffron (*kuṅkuma*).

47a) Having taken fresh turmeric and stirred it with *cāḍacaḍa*, one should place it in fragrant oil. Then, when the superior fragrance has died away, one should cook it a little more; it should be taken up while still fine and ground with *piṣpa* and *raṅgalākṣa*.

Having placed it in fragrant water, and then having added *sajjī* and *ṭaṅkaṇa* for the duration of a moment, one should immerse fragrant substances such as flowers in the lac juice; it becomes saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
Then, take two parts of *tavākṣīra* and one part of *kasūma*, grind both together; thus [is prepared] twenty *ṭaṅkas* and one *nisā*.
Having ground buffalo curd, honey, and sour substances together, O Giver of Boons, one should then form pills (vaṭī) and dry them in the shade for a day and night;
then one should grind them again, grinding them with the juice of *āmalī*.

Again, one should dry it and again pound it. In the center of that, [place] guggulu, oil, and then mustard oil (*kaṭutaila*). Having added an equal amount of *chalīrā* decoction and mustard oil, one should maintain it within the earth; by that, the saturation with oil occurs. Saffron becomes fit for use once twenty parts of vermilion have been added.
First, one should mix it with water and grind it; then, having dried it again, one should grind it once more with oil.

One should rub the *bhavya* [substance]. Having stirred the leaf, one should place it inside a small jar (*kupikā*), seal it, and set it aside. One should hold the oil above. It is red, possessing great power (*mahāsiddha*), and beautiful. Thus is the northern direction.

The primary filament (*kesara*) is three parts; it consists of saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and *kauntumbha*. Having made these together with *tavakṣīra* and *kacūrṇa*, one part of *mālatī* juice should be added.

One should administer an infusion with sour gruel after forming it into pills; having dried them in the shade and again reduced them to a fine powder, one should grind them with Varada oil and make them extremely subtle by adding forty-five parts of [the powder]. One should then grind twelve parts of the potency together with Triphalā.

There, forty-five *maṇas* in total constitute the measure for the jar; therein one should place twenty *dhara*s of saffron. There is beautiful saffron measuring five *cala*s: ten *ṭaṅkas* of *pārā*, ten *ṭaṅkas* of saltpeter (*suhāgā*), fifteen *ṭaṅkas* of cinnabar (*hiṅgula*), and one *maṇa* of flower-salt (*phūla*).
One should boil one *tula* of *ekataila* with a decoction of *karcūra*; the oil will become pungent and fragrant with saffron. (48b)
One should cause the *garuḍa* (emerald) to be repeatedly washed and dried until it becomes dry;
when it is dry, one should grind it on a stone. Having ground it with the essence of *kesūra*, one should add eight parts;
having ground it with the essence of *alatāra*, one should place it in the middle of the *mala* (impurity), remove the hair-like fibers (*aṇḍikā*), and grind it on a stone.

Having placed it in the middle of a mortar, one should pound and knead it. Then, having cast it into mustard oil along with borax and so forth, one should subject it to solar heating (*sūryapāka*) for nine days. With that oil, one should rub all the petals. One *maṇa* (approximately 2.6 kg) yields one *pratisera* of excellent seed-saffron (*bījakuṅkuma*). One should take drops from the flowers of the *bhālu* plant and dissolve them in six *eṣīṇas*.
Thus, taking three parts of *alatāna* and three parts of *rāvaṃtraka* (49a),
one should take three parts of the powder to be used, mix them together, knead them with goat’s urine, and allow them to rest.
Saffron is a fragrant substance. Thus [ends the section on] substances such as fragrances.
One should prepare six palas of the pulp from the interior of a bilva fruit, eight palas of powdered masha beans,
four palas of neem, and two palas of juice.
One should administer one *pala* each of jaggery, guggulu, and ginger;
likewise, the powder of white *guñjā* mixed with the powdered seeds of *gandharva*.
Having carefully ground the substance of black gram flour into a powder,
one should then mix it with the powder of *picumanda* seeds and rub them together.
Hiṅguḍā is the primary [ingredient]. One should maintain it for one month in goat’s milk; Muraha becomes the primary [ingredient]. [This is] the portion for Tavaṣīra.

Take three parts of *aṣoḍagī*, one part of milk, and one part of potent asafoetida as the principal ingredient. These should be processed with a decoction of *kaḍukarāī* for impregnation (*bhāvanā*); with this, one should grind [the mixture]. Having ground it with *gugula*, one should grind it within mica (*abhra*).
Even if the body is afflicted by disease, one should grind it with the juice of *alasaṇa*. A leaf of asafoetida should be added; thus it becomes odorless.

Regarding garlic: on the first day, nine palas of buffalo milk should be taken, along with one pala of *mahāgandha* oil, one pala of *māṣa* powder, four palas each of *ahiśṛṅgī*, *surabhi*, *tāpī*, and *vārāhī*, six palas of *guggulu*, six palas of *gūṇḍa*, four palas of *rājikā*, and two palas of *kacūra*. One should add the seed [of garlic] and refine the boiling oil until it reaches the desired consistency.

First, one should seal it with water; fifthly, having filled a *phūṃṭaḍī* vessel with seeds mixed with *guggulu* resin in a one-fifth proportion, and having kept it in a secret place, it becomes a *ṣadiragūṃdapakṣaḍā*.
One should maintain one *cāvala* (1/4 *tola*) of each of the twenty ingredients and place them in a mortar. One should grind them with milk. [Add] twenty *vīsa* (units) of *guggulu*.

Twenty *palas* of odorless garlic, having made all these into a powder, one should knead it with *guggulu*. Having formed this into a ball (*mardikā*), one should again add powder to the principal [substance].
It becomes fragrant and free from impurities. One should take a large quantity of sulfur, tie it in a cloth pouch (*poṭalī*), and subject it to sweating (*svedayet*).

It should be kept in a *ḍolā-yantra* (swinging apparatus) for one day and night amidst steam in water. In this way, the sulfur is held; it falls drop by drop from the upper part. When placed in milk, purification occurs. This is the best method.
In this manner, one should cause pure sulphur and mercury to be processed.
(50b) Five *ṭaṅkas* of copper and five *suhajanas* [of mercury] are placed in the midst of the juice; the leaf is applied seven times, lime eight times, and *palāśa* [leaves] [are used].
Boil seven times in the juice of *āvilī* and *nimbu* (lemon) along with its seeds;

then wash it again with water. Boil it again for one *prahara* (three hours) in cow’s milk, then wash it once more. Having added an equal amount of sulfur (*gaṃdhaka*) to the copper, maintain it by making it into a powder. This is the *mahābala-cūrṇa* (great strength powder) using fresh juice.

One should take *vartaya* (pills) for the destruction of phlegm (*śleṣman*). Its powder—*valaghanavāka* one *gaḍyāṇa* and *ḍaroha* one *gaḍyāṇa*—should be consumed at dawn; it destroys urinary disorders (*prameha*). Furthermore, with *sāha* (Trigonella corniculata), by its power, [one should take] *sakara* one *gaḍyāṇa* and *vaḍarohagandhajaḍaga* one *gaḍyāṇa* at dawn.
One should consume it;
it destroys chronic wasting disease (*kṣayaroga*). Furthermore, its powder-strength increases [the efficacy of] *śilājatu* and *gaḍūcī*.

One should consume one *vala* of *hiṅgu* (asafoetida); it destroys colic (*śūla*). Furthermore, one should consume four *valas* of its powder along with thirteen *valas* of *śilājatu* and one *pratibhakṣa* of *vacchanāga-bhaṅgaratī*; this destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). This is the *Tāmrabhairava-rasa*. One should place one *pala* of mercury (*rasa*) inside a new crucible (*haṇḍikā*). Then, in each turn...
One should add sulfur; one *pala* of the powder should be used, and one *pala* of purified *vādukī* should be placed on top.
Having applied a layer of clay (*kapāṭamṛttikā*) on top and added one *pala*, one should grind it with that.
Beyond the *culhakā* [furnace], one should ignite the lamp-fire very slowly and gradually.

51b) As long as the vessel remains cool, it should be removed from the fire; once it has been made cool to the touch, one should then have the *vaṭuka* (the recipient) take it. Having reduced it to a fine powder, [one should observe] two days of fasting.
This destroys diseases arising from the three humors (tridoṣa), as well as those caused by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman).

Take one part of mercury (rasa), two parts of sulfur (gandhaka), three parts of copper (śulva), seven parts of mica (mari), one part of poison (viṣa), one part of *ciramaṭhī*, and one part of the bile of a *rohūka* fish. Grind these together with the latex of the *arka* plant. A pill the size of a chickpea (*caṇaka*) should be prepared.
Each single pill destroys sannipāta fever; it destroys fever caused by the three doṣas. Oṃ kāca pāpa ṛṣikasya ṛṣikasya ṛṣikāpūta. (52a)
The Sun Deity; the King Śrīsūrya, son of the Sun Deity; the King Śrīsugrīva, son of Sugrīva; those who carry out his commands;

the sons, the water-dwellers, the sky-goers, the spirits, the *piśācas*, the moving ones, the wandering ones, the hole-dwellers, the mind-stalkers, the artisans, the *ḍākinīs*, the *śākinīs*, the *satis*, and the *sītās*—may they stand at the forefront as mounts.

The Padma, Vānara, Cāla, and Iva-hatta-ṛṣi, moving with great speed, shall become active; let the command of King Sugrīva be issued, and let Brahmā and the others move from their positions. *Oṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Āditya, Vāridī, Dīpa, Dharaṇa, Kanyāka, Ihācāvala, Mudrā, Supārī, Naivedya-dharaṇa, and the rest [are summoned]. Oṃ. *Note: The text provided contains a mixture of Sanskrit mantras and archaic Prakrit/Hindi-style liturgical language. The translation reflects the ritual context of summoning deities and spirits.*

On the seventh lunar day (52b), having recited the mantra, one should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) that have been turned yellow, or alternatively, a lamp made of white mustard seeds (*śvetasarṣapa*). This is the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

[This is] for beauty and so forth, with *eṣaijaupūṃchaishaḥ*: *Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ vada vada vāgvādini namaḥ svāhā*. [Take] *giguḍuvīḍo* (21 times), *ṣirahaṭī*, *rasena*, *kāṃ*, *kākaṭorā*, *kaṣaḍoṭī*, *kaṭoraideve*, *uparipuṭavajramiṭīkādījai*, and *manaśila* (realgar) 3 *ṭaṅkas*; these are to be ground together and placed in a *kaṅkaṭora* (earthen vessel).

Some [are] to be made into a mass of food; one *kaika* measure of *paṭaighāti* is to be taken daily. One *ṭhoka* of *āṇicyāri* is to be taken; one *ṣalova* of *hiḍiḍa* is to be taken. One *ṣirahaṭī* of *kasera*, one *kalarūserū* of *ādhuvicika* is to be held;
one *yañjadhūpa* is to be held. Two *praharas* and three *atha* [of these] are to be consumed. Thus it is said.
It should be prepared as desired:
five *seras* of oil, five *seras* of ghee, and three *seras* of *aṭā*, all combined together; this is the "seven-oil" (*saptataila*) preparation, which should be stirred within [the vessel].

One *sera* of *kīṭikaḍī* (a type of insect or plant product), one *pāvaṇī* of *bhalī* (a medicinal substance), and one *pāuṇī* of *kāuṇī* (a type of plant); adding one *sera* of *vocedeṇa* (a fermented liquid) results in a *sāvaṇā* (a specific preparation).
Adding one *sera* of curd (*dahī*) results in an *aṭāśya-kāvaṇā* (a specific mixture), which becomes clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Thus ends the method for making clarified butter.

One *savāku* (approx. 40g) of *guṇimaṇa* (ginger), one *cāvala* (approx. 80g) of rice, curd, and grinding; with eight *seras* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), it becomes a *ṣāṇḍa* (curry) when rubbed with *duralāi* (long pepper). Thus is the preparation of *ṣāṇḍa*. Ten *seras* of *nivolī* (a type of plant), ten *seras* of garlic, ten *seras* of *araḍolī* (a type of herb), five *seras* of buffalo milk, five *seras* of thickened milk (*dhaṇī*), five *seras* of molasses, and five *seras* of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*); having combined these together, they are to be pounded.
[The substance] becomes asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). Thus ends the preparation of asafoetida.
53b) Five *seras* of marrow and two *rālas* of resin are to be boiled together with one *sera* of oil; [these are] the ingredients for the heating and boiling.

Regarding the casting and purification of mercury (coḍi): it should be purified by casting it into a crucible. This process of casting and purifying within a crucible occurs through heating. As for the procedure: seven supārīs, vermilion, the powder of *karinī*, two packets of cow’s milk, one packet of *dhattūra* and *kerasa*, one packet of *arka* milk, and two *seras* of the juice of hard *kerasa*.
Dūdhūbhi, vāvaṇī, jitupāṇī, hoikorī, hāḍī, drāvaṇī, jāgala, golī, kilāśka, hośtolī, bāndhaṇī, and sirolī. (54a)

The measure is one *deśanī* per day; for three nights, it is one *mūṣī*. Take one *sera* of *vījaśa*, four *maṇas* of *ṭhaṅka*, and seven *ṭaṅkas* of *rāla*; having combined these and melted them together, there will be seven *seras*. When the essence (*sevaṇī*) has become of equal flavor (*samarasa*), it is called *coivālāra-lāvaṇa-maṇa*. [Add] one *ṭaṅka* of *haritāla* and one *ṭaṅka* of *pārā* to the *dhoharika*.

[The preparation] for making pills from milk and *ahi-mardana* [is as follows]: half a *sera* of long pepper (*pippalī*) flour, ten *taṅkas* of cumin (*jīra*), and *viura* [are used] for making the pills. After massaging with *uḍada* oil, again, a heart-shaped (*hṛḍīkorī*) three-long-pepper powder is applied; below it, a protective layer (*pālī*) is placed, and above that, a layer of *cirasu* is applied. Again, a lid (*ḍhakaṇī*) is placed on top and sealed (*leṣu*).
The sun, moon, fire, water, salt, sunlight, and the measure of time (kala) become its stains.

54b) So much is the subtraction of mercury (rasa) from the silver (suhāga). So much is the weight (tolā) [of the silver]; one part (māsa) of mercury and one part of the subtracted silver (degālana), when divided again by a single unit, becomes the amount of the subtracted silver from the silver. [This is] three parts of cinnabar (siṅgaraphaṭa).
Take three *tola* of mercury (*taṅka*), one *tola* of copper (*lohāṭa*), one *vaiḍekai*, and the juice of *magaja-nāli-dūṣa*.

Grind these together with realgar (*siṅgarapha*) and *deṇāsu* (a type of plant) into a paste. This should be applied in the center. In this way, the seed (*bīja*) becomes filled with blackness; it becomes supremely fragrant. Thus is the method for making musk (*kastūrī*).
One should dissolve mana-pradhāna in the midst of oil and drop it into water; it becomes a thin film (paṭī).
Again, when it has been melted in another vessel, the oil produced by this third part [is called] karaṇā-taila.

One-fourth portion should be given to friends, another portion to the dull-witted, and likewise a portion to those who are dear; having thus crushed the *aḍikā* plant together with the others, one should then have it dried.
[The plants are: *kṣīrakanda*, *kṣīramūla*, and *punarnavā*.
The urine of a cow that has not yet calved is the characteristic sign of one who has fathered a child.

The *andhamūṣā* (blind crucible) is prepared with *haiyakāvaṇī*. [It is used for] four *praharas* of heating in a crucible, [using] the urine of a camel (*mūsataikāṭigardabhaka*), and cooking with *vīci*. In the *dolāyantra*, sixty-four *tolakas* of sulfur oil (*gaṃdhakakātailu*) are placed in an iron vessel (*hāḍīretasetī*).
It is filled with iron, and the crucible is covered with various types of earth (*vicidharaṇī*) and heated (*vivirūpāpāvaṇā*).
Togāndhakakātelu-carāvaṇavaśdākātela-ṭaṅka 9; cāraṇā phaṭ kaḍīpāṇī-jaluvahūtanikalaśvaidaikā || 55b)

Take four *taṅkas* of sulfur, two *seras* of oil, and one *kāḍhaṇā* of *unosa* (salt). Place these in a vessel according to the prescribed method and heat them over a fire. Then, add one *sera* of *rohūkā-pitā* (sour gruel) and cook using a *dolāyantra* (swing-oven apparatus) until it is fully processed.
This is the preparation of sulfur-oil.

Take one *sera* of *usādarada* (cinnabar), ten *seras* of *kaṭāhikāra* (mercury), one *sera* less than that (*nine sera*) of *caḍāvaṇāvera* (a specific medicinal substance), and nine *maṣṭakas* of *punah-kunālī-pāvaṇa* (a type of medicinal powder). Grind together *miraca* (black pepper), *piśa* (leadwort), *karidala* (cardamom), *cī* (ginger), and *aḍaṅkaṇa* (asafoetida);

this is the preparation for *kunālī-pāśya*. When mixed with *majjā-pāvaṇī* (medicinal marrow), it becomes a potent remedy. [Add] gold-colored mercury, sulfur, *kaṭakaṇa* (borax), *tāpya* (calamine), and *tuttha* (copper sulfate).
The number of moons (1), eight (8), arrows (5), flavors (6), pairs (2), and qualities (3)— that is, fifty-six (56)—

is the measure of the *jambīra* fruit and *rājaphala*. This, along with mercury (*rasa*) processed into a powder by Siddhas using a crucible (*satvapuṭa*), is combined with poison, pearls, bamboo-manna (*vallaja*), and mercury.

Siddhorasa: This "Laughing-Licked" [preparation], beautiful in all its parts, is declared to be a destroyer of diseases. It overcomes chronic fever, anorexia, consumption, urinary disorders, cough, blindness, hemorrhoids, abdominal ailments, and disorders of the bowels. Thus ends the Sarvāṅgasundara-rasa. [Next is] Kṛṣṇā-sāra-mṛga-śṛṅgaka, as follows:

One should reduce it to a fine powder, place it in a jar, and saturate it with the juice of *sahilamocikā*. Having removed it and heated it over a moderate fire, the virtuous call this substance "Caṇḍeśvara. By giving it with water, along with *vyoṣa* and *karīra*, at dawn or at sunrise, even a chronic fever attains pacification.

Take equal parts of *kuṣṭha*, sulphur, poison (*viṣa*), and one-quarter part of *triphalā*. These should be ground with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* and made into pills the size of mung or black gram. They destroy fever within eight watches or eight praharas.
Thus ends the venerable Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata.
May there always be auspiciousness. May there be auspiciousness.
